transcript.content: Hello, I am Dr. Smith. Could you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Well, um... it's just, I guess what finally pushed me to actually pick up the phone and make the appointment to come in today is that my eating has just been completely all over the place. And I mean, just totally unpredictable. It's so frustrating because, you know, I usually try to keep a somewhat normal routine, but lately... well, some weeks I'll sit down and I barely even touch my dinner. I just look at it and I have absolutely no interest, I just sort of push it around my plate and maybe take a bite or two, and that's it for the whole evening. 

But then, it completely flips, and there are these other nights where... well, I wait until the house is totally quiet, after everyone’s gone to bed, and I just find myself standing in the middle of the kitchen. I don't even turn all the lights on or sit down at the table like a normal person. I just stand right there by the counter eating crackers, and just whatever sweets I can get my hands on. Like, I'll just stand there eating handfuls of cookies or whatever is left in the pantry. It's just so back and forth, going from nothing to just standing in the dark eating everything in sight, and I really didn't know what else to do because it's really starting to bother me...
When you are eating those handfuls of food in the dark, do you feel like you are unable to stop or that you don't have control over what or how much you are eating?

Um, no, I really wouldn't say it's like that. It's not that I can't stop, or that I've lost control of my hands or my mouth or anything dramatic like that. I mean, I know exactly what I'm doing. I'm standing there, usually in my blue slippers—the ones with the hard soles, because the kitchen tile gets so incredibly cold at night—and I'm fully aware that I am eating. 

It's not like a trance or anything. I could absolutely just close the pantry door and walk back down the hall to my bedroom at any second. I just... I choose not to, I guess? It's more like, I'm just standing there, and the house is so incredibly still, you know, where you can hear the refrigerator humming and the clock ticking in the living room, and I just think, well, I'm already here, I might as well have another cracker. And then I have another. I know exactly how many I'm eating, and I know exactly what they are—whether it's the saltines or those little chocolate chip cookies we keep on the middle shelf. 

So, no, I definitely have control. It's not like a runaway train where I'm powerless and just shoving food in my face without thinking. It's not like I wake up the next morning and find a bunch of empty wrappers and wonder what on earth happened. It's just this... this drawn-out process where I keep deciding to have one more, over and over, while I'm just standing there staring into the dark kitchen. I could stop, I just... don't.
Outside of these eating habits, how have you been feeling in terms of your mood, energy levels, and your interest in doing the things you usually enjoy?

Well, my mood... it's just, I don't know, it's been really hard to pin down, honestly. But the main thing I've noticed, and it's been bothering me for a while now, is that my interest in things is just... gone. It's like the color has been drained out of everything. 

I used to have this whole routine, these things that really gave my week structure and joy. Like my book club. We meet every other Tuesday at Sarah's house—she has this gorgeous wrap-around porch, and we always sit out there if the weather is nice, drinking iced tea and discussing whatever historical fiction we chose that month. I used to read the books so carefully, taking notes in the margins, you know, just really looking forward to the discussion. But lately... I haven't even cracked open the last two books. The thought of reading them, of going to the meeting and trying to follow the conversation, it just feels like this enormous chore. 

And it's not just the book club. It's cooking, too. I used to love trying new recipes, spending a whole Sunday afternoon simmering a sauce or baking bread from scratch, getting flour all over the counter. Now, the idea of chopping an onion feels like climbing a mountain. I just look at the recipe and think, what's the point? It's just so much effort. 

Even going to the art galleries downtown, which used to be my absolute favorite thing to do on a Saturday morning... I'd get a coffee, walk through the exhibits, just take it all in. But the last few times I thought about going, I just couldn't muster the energy to get dressed and drive down there. 

And my rose beds... oh, my roses. I've spent years cultivating them, pruning them just right, making sure the soil pH is perfect. I have these beautiful David Austin varieties, the ones that smell like my grandmother's perfume. Usually, I'm out there every morning with my clippers and my gardening gloves, checking for aphids, deadheading the spent blooms. But now, I just look out the kitchen window at them, and I know they need tending, I know the weeds are creeping in, but I just keep putting it off. I tell myself I'll do it tomorrow, or the next day, but I never do. Everything I used to look forward to just feels so heavy now, like an obligation I just want to avoid.
Have you experienced periods like this before in your life, where you felt this same loss of interest and lack of energy, or is this the first time you've felt this way?

Well, yes, I have. I mean, it's not the first time, not by a long shot. It's something that kind of... cycles around, I suppose you could say. I remember periods like this going back years, where I just go through these stretches—and they can last for weeks or even months—where everything just feels so different. 

Like, the whole house just feels gray and heavy, if that makes sense. It's not like the lights are actually dimmer, but it feels like they are. I'll just sit at the kitchen table, the one by the window where I usually like to watch the birds at the feeder, and I'll just sit there feeling completely empty. And the strange thing is, I'll be sitting there feeling this immense weight, this profound sadness almost, even though nothing terrible has happened that day. 

Like, nobody died, the bills are paid, the weather might even be perfectly fine outside, but I just have this sinking, heavy feeling in my chest. I remember one time, maybe three or four years ago, I sat at that same table for almost three hours just staring at the salt and pepper shakers. The salt shaker has a little chip on the bottom edge from when my husband dropped it in the sink, and I just stared at that chip, feeling like I couldn't possibly summon the energy to stand up and make a cup of tea. It just feels like all the air has been let out of the room, and I'm just existing in this heavy, gray space, waiting for it to pass, but not really believing it ever will. So, yes, it's definitely happened before, this same kind of empty, heavy feeling where nothing seems to matter.

During these periods when you feel that heavy, gray emptiness, have you ever felt or heard things that others couldn't, or held beliefs that felt undeniably true even if others thought they were strange or impossible?

Well, um... it’s funny that you ask that, because I don't know about strange beliefs, really, but there is this... this thing that happens. And it does seem to happen when the house is just so quiet and I have that heavy feeling. It usually happens when I’m completely alone. 

Like, my husband will be out, and I'll be in the spare room—I have this little desk in there where I keep all my art supplies from when I used to take classes at the community college. I have all these little plastic bins, you know, the clear ones so you can see exactly what's inside, and I'll be sitting there just sorting through my paints, checking to see which of the watercolor tubes have dried up and which ones are still good. And right while I'm doing that, completely focused on the paints, I will hear my name. Just clear as a bell. Or sometimes it's not my name, it's just a really short remark, like someone saying 'there it is' or 'look.' And it sounds exactly like someone is standing directly behind me, maybe just inches from my shoulder. I'll whip around so fast, fully expecting someone to be standing right there in the room with me, but... there’s never anyone there. The room is completely empty. 

And, well, it’s not just in the house, either. It happens outside sometimes when I'm watering the roses—those David Austins I was telling you about earlier. I have this heavy, galvanized steel watering can, the vintage kind with the long spout, and I'll be pouring the water, just listening to it soak into the mulch, and I'll hear that same voice, just a quick comment right behind my ear. I'll actually drop the watering can sometimes, water splashing all over my shoes and the patio stones, and I'll spin around thinking a neighbor must have walked up behind me on the grass. But I look, and the yard is just completely empty. There's no one there at all. It's just so vivid, though, I can't help but turn around and look every single time.
